prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Philip Morris International Inc." (ticker PM), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "PM", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Philip Morris International Inc.
result.industry: Tobacco and nicotine products (cigarettes and smoke-free alternatives)
markets: International cigarettes (Marlboro, L&M, Chesterfield, Parliament) outside the US
Heated tobacco (IQOS devices and TEREA/HEETS sticks)
Nicotine pouches and oral nicotine (ZYN, General snus)
US smoke-free nicotine (ZYN, and IQOS preparing to launch)

mission.source: PMI Statement of Purpose (pmi.com/statement-of-purpose); purpose first announced in 2016 and refreshed in 2022
mission.plain: Get adult smokers to switch from cigarettes to less harmful smoke-free nicotine products, and eventually stop selling cigarettes.

about.plain: Philip Morris International makes cigarettes like Marlboro and sells them in almost every country except the United States. It also makes newer products that give adults nicotine without burning tobacco, like the IQOS heated tobacco device and ZYN nicotine pouches. It wants smokers to switch to these products and says it plans to stop selling cigarettes one day. Because nicotine is addictive and heavily taxed, its customers keep buying and prices keep rising.
about.customers: Adult smokers and nicotine users around the world, who buy its products through shops, kiosks, gas stations and IQOS stores.
about.everyday: Marlboro, the world's best-known cigarette brand, and the ZYN nicotine pouches popular in the US are both sold by PMI (Altria owns Marlboro in the US).

money.plain: Marlboro, L&M, Chesterfield, Parliament outside the US
IQOS devices and TEREA tobacco sticks
ZYN pouches, especially in the US
Bringing IQOS ILUMA heated tobacco to US smokers

result.summary: Yes. PMI has a wide moat from Marlboro, the world's leading cigarette brand, strong pricing power in an addictive and heavily regulated category, and a dominant lead in heated tobacco, where IQOS holds about 76% of category volume. Its smoke-free products reached $16.9 billion, or 41.5% of 2025 net revenues, and regulation and FDA approval requirements make it hard for new rivals to enter, though US ZYN growth has slowed sharply in 2026 as competition rises.

pricingPower.evidence: In 2025 a favourable price variance of $1,536 million, mainly from higher cigarette pricing, lifted combustible net revenues 2.5% even though cigarette shipments fell 1.5% to 607.4 billion units; in Q2 2026 international combustible pricing was up 10.0% while cigarette shipments still rose 1.1%.

moats.evidence: Marlboro is the world's best-selling international cigarette brand, with a record 11.0% category share in Q4 2025, and IQOS is described by PMI as the second-largest nicotine brand in the markets where it is sold, with 9.6% of combined cigarette and heated tobacco volume in Q4 2025.
Nicotine addiction and habit keep users loyal to their brand, and IQOS users who own the device must buy compatible TEREA sticks, though switching between cigarette brands costs nothing.
One person using IQOS or ZYN does not make the product more valuable to another user.

With $40.6 billion of 2025 net revenues, 67% gross margins and distribution in about 180 markets (smoke-free products in 106), PMI has unmatched manufacturing, distribution and R&D scale outside the US and China.

Advertising bans, high excise taxes and costly regulatory approvals (such as the FDA's MRTP and PMTA processes) limit new entrants, leaving most markets to a few large companies (PMI, BAT, Japan Tobacco, Imperial) and state monopolies.

PMI committed early to replacing cigarettes with smoke-free products (purpose announced in 2016), while rivals more dependent on cigarettes moved slower, helping it win about 76% of heated tobacco volume.

PMI spent years and billions of dollars on heated tobacco science, devices and regulatory dossiers, gaining FDA authorisation of IQOS as a modified risk tobacco product, which rivals have struggled to match.
It owns Marlboro outside the US, the ZYN brand (via Swedish Match, acquired in 2022) and IQOS patents and FDA authorisations, giving it exclusive assets, though competitors have their own brands.

customers.evidence: Over 43 million estimated adult consumers used PMI's smoke-free products at end-2025, heated tobacco unit shipments rose 11.0% to 155.1 billion in 2025, and IQOS held about 70% of Japan's heat-not-burn category, showing strong repeat purchase and loyalty.

talent.evidence: PMI was certified a Global Top Employer by the Top Employers Institute for the tenth consecutive year in 2026 and employs about 84,900 people, but working for a tobacco company deters some candidates and it does not feature on mainstream best-places-to-work lists.

product.evidence: IQOS is the clear leader in heated tobacco (about 76% category volume share) and the only such product authorised by the FDA as a modified risk tobacco product, and ZYN is the leading US nicotine pouch brand; VEEV is a smaller player in vapes.

competitors.name: British American Tobacco
competitors.note: Global rival in cigarettes (Dunhill, Lucky Strike, Pall Mall, Rothmans), heated tobacco (glo), nicotine pouches (Velo) and vapes (Vuse).

competitors.name: Japan Tobacco
competitors.note: Winston, Camel (outside the US) and Mevius cigarettes, Ploom heated tobacco (strong in Japan) and Nordic Spirit pouches; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Altria Group
competitors.note: Owns Marlboro in the US and competes in US nicotine pouches (on!) and vapes (NJOY) against ZYN and IQOS.

competitors.name: Imperial Brands
competitors.note: Davidoff, West, JPS and Winston (US) cigarettes, Pulze heated tobacco, blu vapes and Zone X pouches; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: China National Tobacco Corporation
competitors.note: State monopoly that controls the Chinese market, the world's largest; PMI is largely shut out.

competitors.name: KT&G
competitors.note: Leads South Korean cigarettes and the lil heated tobacco brand; also a PMI partner that sells lil abroad through PMI.

competitors.name: Gudang Garam
competitors.note: Kretek (clove) cigarettes in Indonesia, competing with PMI's Sampoerna brands.

competitors.name: Djarum
competitors.note: Private Indonesian kretek cigarette maker competing with Sampoerna.

competitors.name: ITC Limited
competitors.note: Dominant cigarette maker in India, where PMI's Marlboro is sold through Godfrey Phillips.

competitors.name: Turning Point Brands
competitors.note: Zig-Zag, Stoker's and FRE nicotine pouches in the US.

competitors.name: Juul Labs
competitors.note: Private US e-cigarette maker competing with vapes and nicotine alternatives.

competitors.name: Disposable vape makers (Elf Bar / iMiracle and others)
competitors.note: Mostly private Chinese makers of cheap disposable vapes, many sold illicitly, that compete for smokers switching away from cigarettes.

competitors.name: Illicit and counterfeit cigarettes
competitors.note: Untaxed and fake cigarettes take volume in high-tax markets such as the UK, France and parts of Europe.

estimates.name: Disposable vape makers (Elf Bar / iMiracle and others)

marketShare.market: International cigarettes plus heated tobacco units (excluding China and the US)

threats: Slowing US ZYN growth and more competition in nicotine pouches (Altria's on!, BAT's Velo and others): PMI's US net revenues fell 16.5% organically in the first half of 2026 and Q2 2026 ZYN shipments grew only 1.8%

Tougher regulation and taxes on smoke-free products, such as flavour bans (Poland's characterizing flavour ban) and excise increases (Japan, April 2026), which could close IQOS's tax and flavour advantages
Continued decline in cigarette volumes (guided down 2%-3% in 2026) as smoking falls, while cigarettes still provide about 58% of net revenues
Rivals catching up in heated tobacco, such as Japan Tobacco's Ploom and BAT's glo, and cheap illicit disposable vapes taking smokers
Heavy debt (about $48.8 billion at end-2025) and a stockholders' deficit, which leave less room if profits fall
Litigation and legal risks, including the Canadian (RBH) settlement, which led to a $511 million impairment in Q2 2026, and health-related lawsuits
Geopolitical and currency exposure from selling in about 180 countries, including Ukraine, the Middle East and emerging-market currencies

ceo.name: Jacek Olczak
ceo.background: Polish economist (University of Lodz), joined PMI in 1993 and served as chief financial officer and chief operating officer before becoming CEO in May 2021

c1.evidence: PMI leads the fast-growing smoke-free nicotine category (smoke-free net revenues up 15.0% to $16.9 billion in 2025, about 76% of heated tobacco volume), but tobacco overall is a mature, shrinking industry.

c2.evidence: Smokers choose Marlboro for its brand and IQOS and ZYN for their quality and first-mover lead, backed by billions in R&D and regulatory authorisations that rivals have struggled to copy for over a decade.

c3.evidence: Marlboro and ZYN are household names and PMI is the default leader in international tobacco, but many people do not know the PMI name and few would openly 'recommend' a nicotine product.

c4.evidence: PMI repeats its purpose 'to deliver a smoke-free future' in every report and earns about 42% of revenue from smoke-free products, but it still sells over 600 billion cigarettes a year and its critics see the mission as commercially driven.

c6.evidence: “Marlboro, Big Tobacco, cigarettes, IQOS” - the impression is mostly negative because of smoking's health harms, softened somewhat by its move to smoke-free products.

c7.evidence: The global nicotine market is huge and the smoke-free part is growing fast as smokers switch, but total nicotine use is not growing much, so it rides a shift within a mature market rather than a broad secular boom.

c8.evidence: It can expand smoke-free products into new countries (available in 106 markets) and is preparing to launch IQOS ILUMA in the US, but its earlier push into wellness and healthcare (Vectura, Fertin) produced little.

m1.evidence: Jacek Olczak has a clear picture of a smoke-free PMI, setting goals for smoke-free products to become the majority of revenue and pushing ZYN and IQOS into the US.

m2.evidence: He is a career PMI executive since 1993 who became CEO in 2021, not a founder, though he takes a long-term view of the smoke-free transformation.

m4.evidence: PMI emphasises consumer centricity and its employees, earning Global Top Employer certification for ten straight years, but there is little evidence of a distinctive servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Olczak has continued the smoke-free culture shift started under André Calantzopoulos, adding ZYN through the Swedish Match deal and new IQOS ILUMA devices, rather than building a distinctive invention culture himself.

m6.evidence: He is closely involved in product strategy for IQOS and ZYN, but he has a finance and economics background rather than an engineering one.

m7.evidence: He argues that moving smokers to less harmful products helps public health, but he leads a company that still sells hundreds of billions of cigarettes a year, so critics question stewardship aimed at humanity.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Jacek Olczak at a top university has been reported.

m8b.evidence: Olczak is outspoken on tobacco harm reduction but keeps a fairly low public profile.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2021, net revenues rose from $31.4 billion to $40.6 billion in 2025, smoke-free revenue reached 41.5% of the total, and he closed the $16 billion Swedish Match acquisition that brought ZYN.

m10.evidence: PMI runs cost-efficiency programmes, but there is no particular public reputation for frugality.

c10.evidence: Its products feed nicotine addiction; smoke-free products may reduce harm for smokers who switch, but they do not greatly improve lives the way search or surgical robots do.

p2.evidence: Building heated tobacco devices and winning FDA modified-risk authorisation is technically and legally hard, but the importance of the product to the world is debatable.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 68.1% in 2021 to 67.1% in 2025 (after dipping to 63.3% in 2023) and operating margin fell from 41.3% to 36.6%.

f3.evidence: At December 31, 2025 PMI had $48,835M of debt against $4,872M of cash (about four years of operating cash flow of $12,233M) and a total stockholders' deficit of $8,028M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $12,975M in 2021 to $14,892M in 2025 and operating cash flow from $11,967M to $12,233M, but both fell in 2022-2023 (operating income $11,556M and cash flow $9,204M in 2023).

v1.evidence: IQOS is clearly the leading heated tobacco product (about 76% of category volume) and the only one authorised by the FDA as reducing exposure to harmful chemicals, but smokers can also choose cheaper vapes, pouches or rival brands.

v2.evidence: PMI was certified a Global Top Employer by the Top Employers Institute for the tenth consecutive year in 2026, but it is not ranked on mainstream lists such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: Millions of adult smokers using IQOS and ZYN would miss less harmful alternatives to cigarettes, but the world would not be worse off without its cigarettes, and other companies would fill the gap.
